Working now. Let me gather sources.I've written notes on all 31 verses, but the research is uneven. My tool budget ran out partway through, so several sources you listed never got searched (details at the end).

**What came up**
- **Fullest sources:** the Enduring Word page, the Precept Austin page, and a set of older commentaries (Gill, Wesley, Matthew Henry, Keil & Delitzsch, Constable, Coffman and others). For many of these I only saw short search excerpts, not the full pages.
- **Where Protestant traditions differ:** I didn't find any clear split by tradition. Two disagreements did come up among individual teachers: what v. 1 actually describes, and whether Samson's death was suicide (v. 30).
- **Other views:** I have one Catholic source and one modern scholarship note, which reached me second-hand through Precept Austin. I found nothing Orthodox and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching.

---

## Judges 16 – Research Notes

**v. 1**
- **Traditional:** Samson is clearly sinning. He kept the outward signs of his Nazirite vow while sleeping with a prostitute. He split his life into areas God cared about and areas he thought God didn't. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Gill:** The Targum and some Jewish commentators (Kimchi and others) read the word as "innkeeper," someone running a lodging house. Gill allows that the keeper may have been a prostitute herself, or that Samson met one in her house and was ensnared. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-16.html
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Samson went into a public inn to rest, saw her by chance, and was trapped because he let himself keep looking (he links Gen 3:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/judges-16.html
- **Matthew Henry:** This is the first of two dangerous involvements with prostitutes; he barely escapes this one. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_016.cfm
- **Minority reading (The Gospel Coalition):** The Hebrew "came to her" doesn't have to mean sex. The same phrase in Judg 4:22 (Barak entering Jael's tent) is translated without any sexual sense. Staying with a prostitute was a way to enter a town unnoticed, as the spies did with Rahab (Josh 2). On this view the scene prepares for Gaza's destruction later in the chapter. The article admits most commentators and translations read it as sex. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/what-was-samson-doing-with-a-prostitute-in-gaza/

**v. 2**
- **Gill:** The town's leaders were told, perhaps by people who recognised him or by the prostitute herself. They guarded the town gates rather than surrounding the house, which they may not have known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/judges/16.htm
- **NET Bible note (via Precept Austin):** The rest of the verse suggests they surrounded the town, not the house. If they had known where he was, they wouldn't have needed to guard the gate. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB):** The text doesn't say why Samson came. Unless he was disguised, it was a dangerous exposure in an enemy stronghold. The Gazites felt so sure of him that they waited until morning. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/judges-16.html

**v. 3**
- **Enduring Word:** Despite his sin, God still gave him strength to escape. God used Samson in spite of his sin, not because of it, since God's purpose was bigger than Samson. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Wesley:** Samson may have woken from a warning dream, or more likely from a guilty conscience. Wesley answers why God would empower him right after such a sin in two ways. First, Samson had probably repented in some measure. Second, his strength "was not in itself a grace, but a gift," tied to keeping the Nazirite rule rather than to the state of his heart. Samson carried the gates to encourage Israel and shame the Philistines, not to show off. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/judges-16.html
- **Gill:** He offers the same options for why Samson woke (conscience, a dream, or an inner prompting). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-16.html
- **How far did he carry them?**
  - Constable: The traditional view is about 38–40 miles to Hebron, but many commentators think it means a hill near Gaza facing toward Hebron. Either way, the point was probably to mock Gaza. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-3.html
  - JFB: The hill is el-Montar, and "Hebron" means the Hebron hill country. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/judges-16.html
  - Adam Clarke (Methodist): Samson wasn't a giant, so the town gates were probably fairly small. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-3.html
- **Prophetic reading (Bible.org):** A city depends on its gates, so tearing them off signals Gaza's coming fall. https://bible.org/seriespage/15-samson-brings-down-house-judges-16

**v. 4**
- **Enduring Word:** He falls for the wrong woman again because he didn't guard his heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Matthew Henry:** Some think Delilah was his wife, but Henry suspects an immoral relationship. Whether she was an Israelite or a Philistine is uncertain. Her name stands for anyone who ruins people through flattery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_016.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** He loved Delilah, but she loved money. One quoted source gives her name as meaning "humbling" or "bringing down." Criswell calls this the third example of Samson's moral weakness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** They give her name as "the weak or pining one." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-16.html
- **Coffman:** He suggests she was a temple prostitute connected with Dagon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-16.html

**v. 5**
- **Enduring Word:** 1,100 shekels from each lord was more than 140 lb (63 kg) of silver. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** "Subdue him" means to bend or oppress him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-16.html
- **Precept Austin:** The Hebrew can be read as "subdued in order to be humiliated." From the start Delilah meant to find his weakness and report it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary

**vv. 6–9**
- **Enduring Word:** Because the source of his strength wasn't obvious, he probably wasn't visibly muscular. He could in fact be "bound," by an ungodly woman's affection. Lying to her shows he knew she meant harm. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Coffman:** "The Philistines are here!" was a test to see whether Samson had told the truth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-16.html
- **Precept Austin:** There's no evidence the Philistines actually came out of hiding; the shout tested his story. Like Joseph, Samson should have run (Gen 39:12; 2 Tim 2:22). https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary

**vv. 10–12**
- **Enduring Word:** Romantic attraction warped his thinking. He had no rational reason to stay, and he allowed himself to be bound because he wouldn't leave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Coffman:** Samson apparently didn't live at her house, or he'd have known about the men hiding there. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-16.html

**vv. 13–14**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The Hebrew text seems to be missing words, and commentators debate what dropped out. The three attempts may have been days apart. By letting his consecrated hair be handled, Samson was already presumptuously trifling with God's gift. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/16-13.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch (another page):** Because v. 14 mentions sleep, Delilah probably tied him up the other times while he slept too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-16.html
- **Constable:** "Tightened it with a pin" uses the same Hebrew words as Jael driving the tent peg (Judg 4:21). He also suggests Samson was hinting at his hair, and may have been drunk or drugged while asleep. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-13.html
- **Benson:** A loom was probably in the room, which gave Samson the idea. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/16-13.htm
- **Coffman:** This lie came closer to the truth, a sign he would soon give in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-16.html

**v. 15**
- **Enduring Word:** Samson's heart really was with Delilah. Her accusation was a manipulative projection of her own heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **F. B. Meyer (via Precept Austin):** From this point his heart was taken captive. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary

**v. 16**
- **Enduring Word:** He gave in to nagging just as he did with his Philistine wife (14:15–18). She sinned by manipulating him, and he sinned by giving in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Precept Austin:** The same Hebrew verb for "pressed" appears in both scenes (14:17; 16:16). https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary
- **Gill:** "Sick to death" means he could hardly bear to live. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-16.html

**v. 17**
- **Sermon Bible Commentary:** This was the turning point, his "Rubicon." Samson had physical courage but lacked moral strength, which comes from a living sense of God's presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/judges-16.html
- **Constable:** Samson was so self-confident that he expected God to work on his terms. He undervalued his calling, mirroring Israel's failures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-13.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "All his heart" shows Samson did know where his strength lay. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-13.html

**v. 18**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** "For he has revealed to me all his heart" is the narrator's comment, not Delilah's words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-16.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Delilah made sure she got the money first, "the wages of unrighteousness." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_016.cfm

**v. 19**
- **Enduring Word:**
  - The hair wasn't magic. It symbolised his consecration and covenant with God.
  - It quotes Spurgeon twice: the hair was "the pledge of God's favour," and the devil can shave a believer's locks while he barely notices.
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **C. H. Mackintosh (via Precept Austin):** A single woman achieved what a thousand Philistines couldn't. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary

**v. 20**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Samson said his *strength* would leave him (v. 17), but the narrator says *the LORD* had left him. They call this difference very important. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-16.html
- **Constable:** Losing the hair was only the secondary reason; the real reason was that the LORD had departed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-13.html
- **Enduring Word:** God "departed" in the sense of withdrawing the strength. Samson had treated God's patience as indifference. It quotes G. Campbell Morgan: trying to do God's work after God has withdrawn is "appalling." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Sermon Bible Commentary:** Temptation works gradually, and Delilah wore him down inch by inch. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/judges-16.html

**v. 21**
- **Enduring Word:** Fittingly, his eyes went first, since women attracted him through his eyes. Inward slavery became outward slavery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Matthew Henry:** The Philistines had probably promised Delilah not to kill him. They blinded him because eyes, unlike hair, never grow back. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_016.cfm

**v. 22**
- **Enduring Word:** The regrowing hair was hope in the dungeon. Spurgeon wonders why the Philistines didn't keep shaving him, and imagines Samson hoping to strike one more blow for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **A. F. Muir (Pulpit Commentary sermon):** God may forgive, but the consequences of sin in this life often can't be undone; his eyes were never restored. https://biblehub.com/sermons/judges/16-30.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- **Enduring Word:** Samson's sin brought glory to a false god; leaders' disobedience leads others to deny God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Matthew Henry:** The Philistines credited Dagon even though they had paid Delilah for the betrayal. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_016.cfm
- **Bible Hub (apologetics article):** It cites Philistine inscriptions to Dagon found at Ashdod and Ekron. https://biblehub.com/q/Samson_s_act_What_does_it_reveal.htm

**vv. 25–27**
- **Enduring Word:** A mere boy led him, which again suggests his strength was supernatural rather than natural. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** It explains the building: with the two central pillars gone, the beams and galleries would all collapse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-16.html

**v. 28**
- **Enduring Word:** This is the first time we see Samson pray; he was restored through humbling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Bible Hub, Judges 16:30 commentaries page:** One commentator there sees a "penitent and prayerful spirit," showing he acted as a public magistrate and not out of vengeful suicide. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/16-30.htm
- **Sermon Bible Commentary:** Losing our vision is the penalty for losing our strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/judges-16.html

**vv. 29–30: was it suicide? (Protestant teachers disagree)**
- **Not suicide:**
  - Benson and Poole (Bible Hub): Samson didn't want his own death. His office obliged him to destroy God's enemies and he couldn't do it without dying. This gives no excuse for self-murder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/16-30.htm
  - Constable: martyrdom, not suicide. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-30.html
  - Coffman: he shouldn't be classed as a suicide. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-30.html
  - Precept Austin: compares it to Christ laying down his life (John 10). https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_16_commentary
- **Suicide of a different kind (Enduring Word):** It was suicide, though his aim was to kill Philistines, not himself. It even compares him to modern suicide bombers, but says Scripture doesn't glorify the act. Samson is a *tragic* hero of Hebrews 11:32. Suicide is sin but not the unforgivable sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Christ-like heroism:**
  - Muir and Balgarnie (Bible Hub sermons) see a heroic self-offering for his people. https://biblehub.com/sermons/judges/16-30.htm
  - The Bible Hub apologetics article claims the Targum and Chrysostom saw it as martyr-like obedience. I couldn't check that claim in any primary source. https://biblehub.com/q/Samson_s_act_What_does_it_reveal.htm
- **Type of Christ:** Matthew Henry says Samson, "conquering by death," is a type of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/judges/16.htm The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary lists parallels, such as a miraculous birth and being rejected by his own people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/judges-16.html
- **Another commentator on the Bible Hub page:** "Let me die with the Philistines" may be a fragment of an old song or proverb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/16-30.htm

**v. 31**
- **Coffman (quoted):** The Philistines were in such confusion that Samson's family could recover his body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/16-30.html
- **Enduring Word:** Samson was a loner. He judged 20 years without seeking help, and his life is a picture of wasted potential. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-16/
- **Wesley:** His 20 years overlapped with the Philistine oppression. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes/notes.ii.viii.xi.ii.html

---

**Other views**
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia retells the chapter as history. It calls the theory that Samson is a Hebrew Hercules, or a sun myth, "superficial conjecture." It grants the story comes from ancient national tradition with moral and religious meaning. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13423a.htm
- **Modern scholarship:** Beyond that article's comments and the single NET note under v. 2, I found nothing.

**Not found (budget ran out before I could search):** netbible.org notes, bibleodyssey.org, Orthodox sources (oca.org), Augustine on Samson's death, Lutheran and Pentecostal-specific sources, and anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Ellicott's and the Pulpit Commentary's own verse-by-verse notes are also missing; only a Pulpit sermon page turned up. These would be the next things to look up.
